newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian parties promise end to mayhem after polls.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parties promise end to mayhem after polls.

text.p: President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party and the Socialists challenging it for power drew cheering crowds to final rallies on Friday in Albania's election, each pledging to deliver the country from violence.

Hundreds of armed police surrounded Tirana's Skanderbeg Square in mid-morning as Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano promised a crowd of 5,000 he would end months of lawlessness triggered by the crash of a string of shady investment funds.

"Albania needs peace and calm. It needs the smiles of everybody, especially the children, mothers and sisters. No dictator will take that smile away any more," he said. "We will bring you joy, hope and the future."

Berisha urged a similar number of sometimes frenzied supporters in the same square at sunset to safeguard democracy by keeping his party in power in Sunday's vote and shunning the Socialist "mobs" he said were responsible for the unrest.
His voice reduced to a rasping whisper as it has been throughout the final week of campaigning, Berisha predicted that "every corner of Albania will vote for us".

"Vote for your children, your expectations, your dreams, vote for integration into Europe," he shouted. "Vote for freedom, not for masked mobs. Not for the division of Albania the other side stands for."
Other Democratic Party leaders, standing beneath a large banner reading "Democracy yes, rebellion no", denounced Nano variously as a liar, a Stalinist and a "little Lenin".
Berisha closed his rally by setting off in a cavalcade of honking cars down Tirana's main boulevard to loud cheers.
The election is widely viewed as the last means of establishing order seven years after the fall of one of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regimes.
Some 450 observers have been dispatched to oversee the vote and a 7,000-strong multinational protection force will help keep polling stations safe.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a message read on the Voice of America, urged Albanians to turn out to vote "to chart a better future for your country".

"I too have experienced times of political and economic uncertainty," Albright, born in pre-war Czechoslovakia, said. "The gesture of voting is a very important one for me, for I have witnessed societies where this right was not allowed."

Berisha has pledged throughout the campaign to restore order to the country of 3.4 million within 75 days. Genc Pollo, Secretary General of his Democratic Party, predicted the party would win around 50 percent of the vote but said it was also prepared to become the official opposition if the leftists won.

The rallies mark the end of an electoral campaign waged against the backdrop of increasing anarchy and violence, particularly in the south of the poverty-stricken nation, which remains largely outside government control.

At least eight people were wounded on Thursday night when shooting erupted during an address by Berisha to supporters in Lushnje, about 80 km (50 miles) south of Tirana. The Democrats later blamed leftist extremists for opening fire on the crowd.

The Democrats have found it practically impossible to campaign in the south, accusing Nano's Socialists, reformed successors of the communists, of using armed gangs to incite violence in a desperate effort to win Sunday's polls.
Nano, 45, blames the unrest on the Democrats and claims the Socialists would strive to reimburse investors for their losses, estimated at some $1.2 billion.
Berisha called the early election as part of a pact struck at the height of the disturbances in March to set up an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.

The vote is being held 13 months after the Democrats scored a big victory in Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990. International observers said that vote was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.
